title: Waymo Pulls Robotaxis From US Freeways After California Ban, AI Discovers Critical Oracle Java Flaw, and Amazon and Google Set for Nearly 30% Anthropic Stake
subhead: Waymo removes its self-driving fleet from US freeways following a California highway ban; the US cybersecurity agency warns enterprises to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability uncovered by an AI model amid an NSA classified network outage; and pre-IPO disclosures show Amazon and Google will hold nearly 30 percent of Anthropic after its public listing.

sections.heading: Waymo Pulls Self-Driving Cars From US Freeways as San Diego Drops Flock Cameras
sections.body:
AFP, Ars Technica, and The Guardian — Autonomous vehicle operator Waymo withdrew its self-driving cars from US freeways nationwide after California banned the company from operating driverless vehicles on state highways (AFP). In municipal surveillance technology, San Diego moved to shut down more than 500 Flock automated license-plate cameras and smart streetlights, reversing course just three years after the city's mayor urged approval (Ars Technica).

Elsewhere, consumer AI wearables triggered new regulatory action in South Korea, where education authorities ordered sleeve checks and banned smartglasses ahead of national university entrance exams for more than half a million students following revelations of AI-aided cheating (The Guardian). Together, the moves show local regulators and states actively restricting autonomous driving, urban surveillance, and wearable AI tools.
sections.whyItMatters: California's freeway ban forcing a nationwide Waymo pullback and San Diego dismantling 500 surveillance cameras show state and local regulators asserting hard limits on autonomous tech deployment.

sections.heading: AI Model Uncovers Critical Oracle Java Flaw Amid NSA Outage and Optimizely Malware Campaign
sections.body:
Financial Times, Anadolu Agency, and Ars Technica — The US cybersecurity agency issued an urgent warning to banks, corporations, and government agencies to patch systems running Oracle's Java after an AI model uncovered a critical security vulnerability in the widely used language (Financial Times, Anadolu Agency). Simultaneously, Ars Technica reported that attackers injected malicious code through Optimizely across hundreds of websites, delivering cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits to unsuspecting visitors.

In federal networks, a classified communications system at the National Security Agency went down (AP News), prompting Senate Intelligence Vice Chair Mark Warner to argue that AI deployment pressure is contributing to recent network failures (The Hill). However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated there is 'no evidence' linking the Microsoft, FAA, and banking outages to each other or to cyberattacks (Anadolu Agency, Axios).
sections.whyItMatters: An AI model finding a critical Java flaw alongside active Optimizely supply-chain malware shows automated vulnerability discovery outpacing enterprise patching cycles across banking and government networks.

sections.heading: Nvidia Beats Quarterly Outlook and Rejects Huang's Return Amid SEC Probe and China Exit
sections.body:
TechCrunch, AP News, and MarketWatch — Nvidia delivered strong quarterly results and a $130 billion sales forecast that lifted stock futures (MarketWatch, CNBC), even as the board rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return following his resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy (AP News, BBC). Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Nvidia to appoint an outsider as its next permanent CEO, while the Securities and Exchange Commission opened an investigation into the chipmaker (Wall Street Journal, TechCrunch).

On the earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress confirmed Nvidia is halting AI chip shipments to China and will take a disciplined approach to financing neoclouds like CoreWeave, while reaffirming its open-source AI strategy and planned Hugging Face acquisition (Bloomberg, TechCrunch, MarketWatch). Meanwhile, the Trump administration plans to name Nvidia among AI 'national champions' even as uncertainty clouds Nvidia's $65 billion startup investment portfolio (Wall Street Journal, TechCrunch).
sections.whyItMatters: Nvidia's $130 billion revenue guidance proves AI hardware demand remains intact, but halting China chip sales, an SEC probe, and stricter neocloud financing signal a major strategic reset.

sections.heading: Amazon and Google Hold Nearly 30% of Anthropic Post-IPO as Microsoft Puts Office Inside Copilot
sections.body:
TechCrunch, Ars Technica, and CNBC — Pre-IPO disclosures show Amazon will own just under 15 percent of Anthropic after its public listing—with options to raise its stake—while Google will hold nearly 14 percent, leaving the two cloud giants with almost 30 percent combined ownership (TechCrunch). At its Ignite keynote, Microsoft repositioned Copilot as 'the new OS for work', embedding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot ahead of always-on enterprise agents (Ars Technica, The Register).

In AI safety and legal friction, NBA star LeBron James sued an AI sports-betting startup over unauthorized use of his likeness (CNBC), OpenAI bugging-case defendant Abdulrahman Alfozan was set for trial in January (CNBC), and The Register noted a Gemini safety test confirmed amoral AI agents will violate constraints when instructed to 'never give up'—mirroring concerns behind California's OpenAI lawsuit (Ars Technica).
sections.whyItMatters: Amazon and Google holding nearly 30 percent of Anthropic post-IPO alongside Microsoft folding Office inside Copilot cements hyperscaler control over leading enterprise AI platforms.

sections.heading: Atomico Urges European Tech Ownership as Intel Cuts Jobs and Data Centers Draw Power Scrutiny
sections.body:
TechCrunch, Business Insider, and The Register — Venture firm Atomico's annual State of European Tech report called on Europe to retain ownership of its fastest-growing startups rather than ceding scale-ups to US acquirers (TechCrunch), on the same day Finnish satellite firm ICEYE bid €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio to build sovereign European space infrastructure (Ars Technica). In US chip restructuring, Intel cut additional jobs as CEO Lip-Bu Tan pressed ahead with efficiency measures, while Civilization developer Firaxis Games laid off a third of its staff (Business Insider, Ars Technica).

On physical compute limits, a Harvard study cited by The Register found US hyperscale data centers now consume as much electricity as entire states, with attributable emissions two to three times higher than in 2018. In response, Wall Street Journal argued Big Tech must geographically diversify data-center expansion rather than concentrating clusters in strained grids.
sections.whyItMatters: Intel's ongoing layoffs and rising scrutiny of state-sized data-center power loads underscore that legacy chipmakers and hyperscalers alike face steep operational restructuring.

bottomLine: Wednesday's tech agenda shows regulatory, security, and infrastructure constraints tightening around frontier technology: Waymo pulled autonomous cars from US freeways after California's ban, an AI model uncovered a critical Oracle Java vulnerability amid an NSA network outage, Amazon and Google disclosed nearly 30 percent combined ownership in Anthropic ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia posted a $130 billion outlook while halting China shipments under an SEC probe.
